ALCUBIERRE METRIC / NUMERICAL LIGHT PATHS

THE MODEL · TIME PAUSED WHILE OPEN

One spacetime.
Different views of it.

Optical shows received light. Layout shows current coordinates. They share the same ship position, heading, speed setting and clock; F changes how the scene is drawn.

Light from the ship, Sun and planets

Past-directed null rays follow a spherical steady Alcubierre metric. The nearest opaque hull or Solar surface ends the ray. Planet positions and orbital velocities are evaluated at the emission time, including the analytic exterior travel before and after the curved region. The Sun and planets occlude one another and the ship.

ds² = −dt² + dx² + dy² + [dz + v(1−f)dt]²
c = R = 1 · σR = 5
f(r) = [tanh σ(r+R) − tanh σ(r−R)] / [2 tanh σR]

In the local Eulerian frame, a prescribed planet has velocity V = W − vf ez, where W is its orbital velocity in the exterior frame at emission. The observed/source frequency ratio is g = exp(−L)√(1−|V|²)/(1+n·V). L is the ray's log energy and n its past-directed local spatial direction. This reduces to the existing comoving hull formula and to ordinary Doppler shift in the exterior. All optical surfaces and the sky use bolometric g⁴ with optional center-view exposure assistance and gentle night-side surface fill. The fill is an illustrative visibility aid, not physical extra sunlight.

The Solar System uses one size/distance scale: R = 1 million km and R/c = 3.33564 seconds. Its clock advances one physical second per real second while playing. Mean distances, diameters and orbital periods come from NASA NSSDCA; phases and circular coplanar paths are illustrative, not a current ephemeris.

What is still a prescribed model

  • Speed and heading changes use successive steady bubble snapshots. The full accelerated metric history and matter backreaction are not simulated.
  • Planetary paths are prescribed test sources, not matter evolved through a warp wall. A nearest surface event whose prescribed velocity is not timelike is censored as unresolved/dark; it never reveals the sky as if the body were transparent. Direct warp-wall encounters do not model a planet's physical response.
  • Solar and planetary gravitational lensing are not added to the Alcubierre metric. Surface patterns and day/night radiance are prescribed artwork, not a full reflected-light, spectral or atmospheric transport calculation. The distant star/galaxy sky is artwork at infinity, so translation alone gives it no parallax.
  • The hull is schematic and tied to bubble scale; the Sun and planets retain the common measured Solar scale. The bridge remains an ideal panorama without its enclosing hull blocking the view. An outside orbit samples instantaneous Eulerian frames; camera-follow and release are inspection tools, not a complete spacecraft observer worldline.

Numerical resolution and verification

Fourth-order Runge–Kutta integrates the null rays, with adaptive steps and shorter steps near surfaces. Swept relative segments test moving spheres, so a small body cannot simply pass between ray endpoints. Surface events are refined on the numerical path. Exterior travel is analytic beyond 3.2 R, neglecting a shape-function tail below 3×10⁻¹⁰. Integration is bounded to 4096 scene steps or 48 R/c inside that region; unresolved rays are dark, not a precision horizon measurement.

External and Solar bridge views use a finite angular scene map. Mixed opaque/background cells are retraced at display resolution, and exterior planets are also tested at display resolution after the cached exit ray. All-surface cells interpolate event data. Tiny off-axis images, caustics and facet edges can still be underresolved. Solar maps update with the source epoch while flying; pausing time allows coherent tiled refinement to 513 samples without combining different orbital times.

Checks reproduce Clark, Hiscock & Larson's exact transverse invariance and axial ratio 1+v, including 51 at 50c. An independent canonical-momentum Dormand–Prince solver checks 78 selected sky rays through 100c and curved finite-source events. The 50c comparison uses published equations and exact limits, not a digitized published 50c image match. Actual GPU checks compare source classification, emission time, position and frequency through 50c on both backends. Numerical agreement tests the stated model; it does not establish exact physical accuracy.

Camera and coordinate references

The bubble's coordinate center is the ship's current position. Layout draws that wire sphere with the current ship and planet positions. Optical draws the delayed images and contains no current-position wireframe. Strong lensing can move or magnify the ship image, and some superluminal views receive no hull light. Those are distinct from camera controls.

IJKL looks in either view. Outside drag defaults to orbit, Shift/right-drag pans, and Shift+IJKL orbits the selected current focus; C recenters look without moving the observer. Steering changes the ship, not the outside camera's world bearing. A following camera naturally keeps the ship near the same coordinates on screen; the clock, distance flown and range now show transport. Release observer in Camera makes the camera stay at a fixed location. HUD arrows, target rings and the map always use positions now; they do not mark the bent optical image. O looks toward the selected current target without moving the ship or camera position.

Rendering and performance

Auto prefers WebGPU and falls back to WebGL 2. The browser selects the Radeon adapter and its Metal/OpenGL translation path; the Site cannot force native Metal. One 4096 × 2048 sky and one active graphics context are retained. Adaptive quality adjusts angular sampling and can reduce pixel resolution for expensive views. High detail keeps the sharper fixed pixel budget; Low reduces it further. At most two submitted frames remain outstanding. Press T to measure this session's actual submitted-frame intervals; around 60 fps is a target, not a guarantee.

Guided tour

Play tour starts one continuous two-minute Solar System flight. The observer glides between the bridge, the bubble, Earth and Jupiter with no cuts, fades or world resets during the flight. Speed and steering use the ordinary controller. Planet camera excursions are inspector movements, not the ship's path or a fully evolved observer worldline. Exit or any flight action preserves the observer pose and actual ship speed. Resume continues from your current Solar flight; a fresh tour sets up a new Solar departure. Help holds the tour clock.

One speed, two views

The large speed is the bubble speed in the current simulation snapshot. Set speed takes effect immediately; with course assist enabled it is a limit and the readout shows the assisted speed. Pause holds the clock, positions and orbital phase while retaining that speed's optical image. Settings panels also hold time and say so. Change speed while paused to compare snapshots, then resume with Space.

Optical shows received light: ship, planets and sky use the same past-null paths. Layout is a current-position diagram with an optional centered bubble shell. It does not claim to be another optical observer. F preserves flight state and camera, so the difference you see comes from these two representations.

Look without fighting the ship

Bridge drag and IJKL look. Outside left-drag defaults to Orbit around the current focus; Shift/right-drag pans in the screen plane. The wheel zooms and Shift-wheel changes FOV. IJKL freely looks and Shift+IJKL orbits. Y / Frame bubble restores a rear view and follows speed with a larger distance at high warp so the distortion stays within the field of view. Manual zoom or pan takes over framing. The Drag: look/orbit button also changes the outside pointer action, including on touch screens. C resets look only; Camera → Frame bubble moves the observer back to its rear following preset. Steering does not rotate the outside camera's world bearing. Camera focus offers Follow ship, Orbit selected target and Release observer. Orbit target moves only the camera; the ship continues its flight. While following, the ship can remain still on screen even at 50c. The distant sky has no translation parallax. Read Distance flown, the clock and the target's Range now to see progress, or release the observer.

Navigation and true scale

HUD target rings, edge arrows and the map use current positions in both Optical and Layout views. Gold marks the selected target; visible planet labels can also be selected. BEHIND means the target is behind the camera. O or Look at target points only the camera toward its current navigation position. The steering line gives left/right and climb/descend directions relative to the ship, independently of camera look. Optical images may arrive from a different direction. N chooses a target; P steers toward its current position, slows while turning and brakes on approach. Solar targets hold near their standoff. Disengaging P or steering manually keeps the actual assisted speed instead of jumping to the old cruise limit. Guides remain available in manual flight; hiding them does not disable assist. Choose Flyby & release for an offset passage that keeps the entire body outside the 3.2R curved-region cutoff with a margin. Planned center separation is 1.4 × (4R + body radius); R is one million kilometres. The controller slows for turns, checks each real-frame travel segment against all Solar bodies, eases steering on departure, then hands back the actual speed and heading. Starting inside clearance first triggers a slow outward recovery. Camera framing stays yours. This is geometric navigation in the prescribed simulation, not a physical collision-avoidance certification. Approach & hold remains available; manual flybys can also use the HUD guides. Map scale is explicit and does not zoom with speed. The small 3D ship/world-frame display shows current attitude.

World → Solar System uses measured sizes and mean distances at one scale: R = 1 million km. One physical second of flight advances one second of the Solar clock. Planet cruise presets range from about3km/s (0.00001c) to0.01c; the precise field accepts six decimal places. Solar Q/E uses smaller steps below0.1c, while Shift changes5c for long trips. Circular orbits have illustrative initial phases. View planet provides a close outside observer around the selected planet without changing the ship's location. Camera / FOV → Visibility assist keeps night-side surface detail readable; Fixed exposure can leave it dark. Visit / inspect explicitly repositions the ship about eight planetary radii away (minimum 20,000 km), sets speed to zero and pauses. It is not a simulated trip.

Radius, wall and limits

R is the bubble radius; σR = 5 gives a wall transition scale near 0.2R. The R key separately resets flight. The shell is a coordinate guide, not luminous material. Optical rays include planetary emission-time positions and frequency shifts, but solar gravity, full accelerated flight history and matter's response to a warp wall are omitted. Invalid prescribed material events are dark/censored. Physics contains the equations, source checks and remaining resolution limits.

Pause to inspect the sharper map after refinement. Camera / FOV also exposes viewing angle, distance and exposure assistance. Low quality reduces display resolution if your device needs it. T runs a 10-second frame-pacing measurement.
